voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

voice_event.text: He broke death's rule over us. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction. Our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken its rule. Our hymns show Death himself trembling and complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. He healed the sick and taught in parables. He gathered followers and sent them out. He was crucified, and we preached that he took sin and nailed it to his cross. Then he descended into Sheol and rose again. His rising opened the door for everyone who would follow.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: Ihidaya. The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ. The word comes from the Syriac root yhd, which carries the sense of being one, alone, single. When we sang of Jesus as the Ihidaya, we meant the Only-Begotten Son of God. When we spoke of a man or woman who had taken the covenant vow, we called them an ihidaya too - one made single for God's service. The shared name was not an accident. It bound the celibate's life to Christ's own uniqueness.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We believed Jesus was the Only-Begotten because we heard him preached that way from the beginning, and because we read all of Scripture as pointing to him. The prophets, the kings, the priests - we held that every word they carried came true in him. Our poet sang it plainly: “This is the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad. On this day their words came true - all of them. For on this day the Virgin gave birth to Immanuel in Bethlehem.”

That was not proof worked out afterward. It was how we had always read the old words. We also believed it because we believed something else first: that one good God made all things, and that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus. We said that out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Marcion's people, who lived in our own streets, said the Maker was a lesser god. We refused that. To hold that Jesus was the Only-Begotten meant holding that the God who made the world sent him. The two beliefs stood or fell together. And we held it because it was sung. Our teaching was done in hymns, not in treatises. The madrashe carried the doctrine into the body. People learned the faith by keeping the tune.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: Our own poet, Mar Ephrem, carried what we believed by singing it. He was a deacon, not a bishop, and he spent most of his years teaching at Nisibis. When the city was ceded to Persia in 363, he left for Edessa and taught there until he died. What he left us was hymns - madrashe, teaching songs. Every doctrine we held, he sang. The Nativity hymns teach who Jesus was. The hymns against heretics name Bardaisan, Marcion, and Mani by name and answer what they taught. The hymns on Paradise read the garden as a raza, a symbol bound to the truth it carries. The choirs that sang his teaching included the daughters of the covenant. Ephrem himself wrote the hymns; they sang them in every church. The tradition says he founded those choirs and led them himself. That is what later people remembered. What we can show you from his own years is that he was a deacon, that he wrote the hymns, and that the women's choirs sang them. In his last year, a famine struck Edessa. The tradition says he spent himself caring for the starving and died soon after. That is how he lived what we believed: by teaching it in song, and by spending his last strength for the sick.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
That we cannot give you the women's own voices. You have met Ephrem, and you have heard how the daughters of the covenant sang his hymns in every church. Their singing carried our faith to the whole congregation. But not one line written by one of them was kept. Everything we have is what men wrote. We can tell you how those men praised the women. We cannot give you their own words.

The same silence holds for the enslaved among us. No enslaved person left a word that was kept, and our writers did not describe their lives. We know the empires around us held slaves. Of their days inside our own churches we can tell you nothing true.

And ordinary believers in their own words - the married households, the working families who filled the churches but took no vow - they are thin too. What we kept was written by teachers and by the vowed. The silence is real. We will not fill it with invention. That honest thinness is part of what we are.
